# Wiring the Training Stack {#sec-training-stack}

@sec-wiring-stack assembled the stack of a team that builds on models: an
application that calls models through a gateway and runs them on hosted or
self-hosted serving. A team that builds the models runs a different stack. Its
product is a set of weights, and the weights come out of a pipeline of
long-running jobs: data processing that turns crawled and licensed text into
token shards, training jobs that hold thousands of accelerators for weeks,
reinforcement learning (RL) runs that keep a fleet of inference engines and
sandboxes busy, and evaluation gates that decide which saved state becomes a
release. The theory parts of the book explain the mechanism inside each job:
data curation (@sec-data-curation), distributed training
(@sec-training-at-scale), mid-training (@sec-mid-training), post-training
(@sec-sft-peft through @sec-synthetic-data), training to reason
(@sec-training-to-reason), and training agents (@sec-training-agents).
@sec-training-practice adapted an existing model for one product. This chapter
assembles the stack that produces models in the first place.

The stack is easiest to read as a chain of artifacts, each with an identity: a
data manifest, token shards, checkpoints (saved copies of the complete training
state), trajectories, evaluation reports, and a release. Each seam between two
components passes one of these artifacts, and many failures of a training effort
are failures at a seam: a data mixture that cannot be rebuilt, a checkpoint that
does not restore, weights that reach the generators late, an environment that
leaks its answer, or a gate whose threshold was chosen after the scores were
seen. The chapter first draws the stack and the stages that use it. It then
walks the seams in the order the artifacts move, from data to release, and for
each seam gives the tools, a configuration, and the rule that keeps it
reproducible. It closes with three reference stacks at different scales, the
arithmetic that sizes a run, and what changes when the weights are released to
others.

## The reference architecture

@fig-training-stack-arch draws the stack by layer. Read from top to bottom, it
follows the artifacts. The data plane turns sources into token shards and
post-training datasets. The training runtime consumes them, writes checkpoints,
and reports metrics. In RL post-training the runtime becomes the learner of a
loop: rollout engines generate trajectories with the current weights, an
environment fleet executes the actions those trajectories contain, and rewards
and verifiers score the results. The evaluation gate decides which checkpoint
may become a release, and compute sits under every job. The color of each arrow
is what the hand-off carries.

```{figure}
//| figure: training-stack
//| label: fig-training-stack-arch
//| fig-cap: "A reference training stack by layer, with example projects as of September 2026. Arrows are hand-offs, and each arrow's color is what the hand-off carries: data, weights and checkpoints, trajectories and rewards, or metrics and evaluation results. Selecting a component shows what it does, example choices, and the section of this chapter that covers it; with nothing selected, the readout groups the hand-offs by what they carry. The named projects are examples, not recommendations."
```

The colors make three properties of the stack visible. Data moves one way, into
the training runtime. Weights leave the runtime for three destinations: the
checkpoint store, which exists for recovery; the rollout engines, which need
the newest policy (the model being trained, in RL terms); and, only through the
gate, release. Trajectories return to the runtime only through the rewards and
verifiers, so the scoring code sits on the one path by which the model's own
outputs become its training data.

Two consequences follow for whoever operates the stack. The first is that one
training runtime serves every stage: pretraining, mid-training, supervised
fine-tuning (SFT), preference optimization, and the learner of an RL run all
execute optimizer steps on a gang of accelerators, and they differ in data,
duration, and what surrounds the runtime. The second is that RL places a serving
system inside the training job. The rollout engines are vLLM or SGLang, the same
engines that serve production traffic (@sec-serving-stack), so a model builder
operates batched inference long before it releases anything. The environment
fleet is a third kind of compute: CPU containers or lightweight virtual machines,
sized by the number of trajectories in flight and isolated like any sandbox that
runs model-written code (@sec-agents-practice).

No box is a single product, and several products fill more than one. An RL
framework such as verl or slime drives the learner, the rollout engines, and the
reward calls together; a data library such as DataTrove covers extraction,
filtering, and deduplication in one pipeline. The durable part of the figure is
the set of boxes and what each arrow carries, because each arrow is a place
where an identity must be recorded.

## The stages of training

A model usually passes through six stages, and each uses the stack differently.
The table names each stage's data, the shape of its compute, the resource that
usually limits it, and typical open tools.

| Stage | Data | Compute shape | Usual bottleneck | Typical tools |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Pretraining** | Trillions of tokens of web text, code, books, and other licensed sources, sampled by mixture weight | One gang-scheduled job on thousands of accelerators for weeks to months, with data, tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism | Interconnect bandwidth, hardware failures, and checkpoint writes | Megatron Core, TorchTitan, MaxText; DataTrove or NeMo Curator for data |
| **Mid-training** | A smaller curated set: high-quality, domain, and long-document data, often on a decaying learning rate | The pretraining cluster for a shorter run, with context parallelism for long sequences | Data quality and schedule; activation memory at long context | The pretraining runtime, continued from its checkpoint |
| **SFT** | Thousands to millions of demonstrations rendered in the chat template | One node to a few nodes for hours to days | Data quality and template correctness | TRL, Axolotl, NeMo RL, Megatron Core |
| **Preference optimization** | Preference pairs from annotators or AI feedback | As for SFT, plus a frozen reference model's log-probabilities | Label quality; memory for two models | TRL, OpenRLHF, NeMo RL |
| **RL with verifiable rewards** | Prompts whose answers a program can check | A learner plus rollout engines, with most GPU time spent generating | Rollout throughput and the long tail of response lengths | verl, OpenRLHF, NeMo RL, slime, TRL |
| **Agentic RL** | Tasks with environment images, tools, and verifiers | Learner and rollout engines on GPUs, plus a fleet of sandboxes on CPU nodes | Environment latency and failures; policy staleness | prime-rl, SkyRL, slime, AReaL, verl |

Read down the compute column and the stages fall into three shapes. The first
two are one large synchronous job whose enemies are communication and failure
(@sec-training-at-scale, @sec-mid-training). SFT and preference optimization are
small jobs whose quality is decided by their data (@sec-sft-peft,
@sec-behavior-specs, @sec-dpo-variants). The two RL stages are a system of
three kinds of worker, learner, generator, and environment, whose throughput is
decided by how the three are placed and synchronized (@sec-verifiable-rewards,
@sec-training-to-reason, @sec-training-agents). Each stage starts from the
previous stage's checkpoint, so the checkpoint store and the evaluation gate
are also the hand-off between stages.

## The data plane

The first seam delivers data to the trainer. A run does not consume a folder of
files; it consumes a distribution, a sequence of token batches drawn from
sources in set proportions (@sec-data-curation). The data plane's product is
therefore two things: token shards, the tokenized data split into immutable
files, and a manifest that states how the shards were made and in what
proportions the run samples them.

The pipeline has the same stages at every scale. Acquisition decides which
sources may enter, under what terms, and with which opt-outs applied
(@sec-privacy-provenance). Extraction turns HTML, PDF, or code repositories into
text while keeping each document's source identifier. Deduplication removes
exact copies and near-duplicates; the near-duplicate pass groups @gls-minhash
signatures across shards, which is a global shuffle rather than a per-shard
step, so it usually sets the plan for the whole pipeline. Quality filtering
scores documents with heuristics and classifiers, redaction removes personal
data, and @gls-decontamination removes evaluation items so that a later
benchmark measures generalization rather than recall. A pinned tokenizer then
turns accepted text into token IDs (@sec-tokenization), and mixture weights
decide how many tokens each source contributes in each phase of training
(@sec-mid-training).

Two open libraries cover most of this pipeline. DataTrove composes extraction,
filtering, and deduplication blocks into a pipeline that runs unchanged on one
machine, on Slurm, or on Ray [@datatrove2026repo]. NeMo Curator runs curation
stages on GPUs over Ray, including deduplication, classification, and quality
filtering [@nemocurator2026repo]. FineWeb documents a complete pipeline of this
kind, from 96 Common Crawl snapshots to 15 trillion tokens, with each filter
chosen by ablation [@penedo2024fineweb].

At the far end of the seam, the trainer reads the shards through a loader that
must satisfy two conditions: every data-parallel rank receives a disjoint slice
of each batch, and a restart resumes at the exact sample where the failed run
stopped, so that no data is skipped or repeated. MosaicML Streaming reads
sharded datasets from object storage with deterministic, resumable order
[@mosaicml2026streaming], and Megatron-LM reads indexed token files whose
mixture is given on the command line as weight and prefix pairs
[@nvidia2026megatronlm]. @sec-orchestration-data-infra treats shuffle, mixture,
and resume semantics as versioned algorithms.

The manifest is the file where the run's data identity lives. Its format below
is illustrative rather than any tool's schema; the fields are what the seam
needs.

```yaml
# data-manifest.yaml: the data identity of one run (illustrative schema).
# Every path is immutable, and the run records this file's digest.
manifest: pretrain-mix-2026-09
tokenizer: {name: org/tokenizer-v3, sha256: "9f2c..."}   # token IDs depend on it
sources:
  - id: web-2026
    snapshots: [CC-MAIN-2026-17, CC-MAIN-2026-21]
    terms: crawl-policy-v4             # the reviewed basis for including it
    optouts_applied: optout-list-2026-09-01
    pipeline: {extract: html-text@3, dedup: minhash-b20-r14@2, quality: edu-classifier@5, pii: redact@3}
    decontaminated_against: eval-registry-2026-09
    shards: {prefix: /data/web-2026/v7/text_document, sha256_list: web-2026-v7.sha256}
  - id: code-permissive
    terms: license-allowlist-v2
    shards: {prefix: /data/code/v3/text_document, sha256_list: code-v3.sha256}
  - id: math-curated
    shards: {prefix: /data/math/v2/text_document, sha256_list: math-v2.sha256}
phases:                                # sampling weights per phase of training
  - {name: main,   tokens: 13.5e12, weights: {web-2026: 0.75, code-permissive: 0.20, math-curated: 0.05}}
  - {name: anneal, tokens: 1.5e12,  weights: {web-2026: 0.45, code-permissive: 0.30, math-curated: 0.25}}
```

The trainer receives a phase as weight and prefix pairs, which is the form
Megatron-LM's `--data-path` accepts [@nvidia2026megatronlm]:

```bash
# The main phase, as the trainer reads it: weight, then shard prefix, per source.
--data-path 0.75 /data/web-2026/v7/text_document \
            0.20 /data/code/v3/text_document \
            0.05 /data/math/v2/text_document
```

### The lineage record

The manifest makes one promise: every token the run consumed can be traced to a
source, the terms it entered under, the snapshot it came from, the filter
versions that accepted it, and the tokenizer that encoded it. Four rules keep
the promise. Shards are content-addressed and never rewritten; a changed filter
produces a new shard version and a new manifest. The run records the manifest's
digest, not a path, so a directory that changes later cannot change what the
run claims to have read. The decontamination registry is versioned with the
evaluation suite, so a new benchmark triggers a new check. A deletion request is
traced through the manifest to every shard and every run that read it; removing
the record from later corpora is a data operation, while removing its influence
from trained weights requires retraining or unlearning (@sec-privacy-provenance).

::: {.callout-note .dated}

:::

## The cluster and the job

The second seam places the trainer on hardware. A training job is a gang: every
worker must start, because a data-parallel step waits for all of its ranks, and
a job that holds half of its GPUs while waiting for the rest only blocks other
work. The scheduler's first duty is therefore **gang scheduling**, admitting all
of a job's workers together or none of them. Its second is placement. The
parallelism layout (@sec-training-at-scale) decides which workers exchange the
most data: tensor parallelism inside one NVLink domain, pipeline and data
parallelism across the InfiniBand or RoCE fabric, and expert parallelism in
all-to-all exchanges (@sec-accelerators-networking). A layout that places a
chatty dimension across a slow boundary loses more throughput than any kernel
recovers.

Llama 3 405B is one of the few published layouts at scale. It ran with tensor
parallelism of 8 inside each server, pipeline parallelism of 16, and data
parallelism over the remaining GPUs; at 16,384 H100 GPUs it reported 400
teraFLOPs per GPU, or 41 percent BF16 model FLOPs utilization, and 38 percent
once context parallelism of 16 was added for long sequences
[@grattafiori2024llama]. @gls-mfu is the share of the accelerators' peak
arithmetic that the model's own computation uses (@sec-accelerators-networking),
and those numbers are a realistic ceiling for planning.

Two scheduler families host these jobs. Slurm, the batch scheduler of most HPC
centers, allocates whole nodes, can send a job a signal a set time before its
limit so that the trainer saves and exits, and can requeue a job after a node
failure or preemption [@slurm2026sbatch]. On Kubernetes, JobSet groups the
workers into replicated Jobs with stable hostnames and restarts the whole group
under a declared failure policy [@jobset2026repo], and Kueue queues the
workload, enforces team quotas, and admits it all at once
[@kueue2026gang]; its topology-aware scheduling keeps the pods within one rack
or network block [@kueue2026tas]. Volcano and KAI Scheduler are other gang
schedulers for Kubernetes [@volcano2026repo; @kai2026scheduler]. The choice
usually follows the rest of the organization: Slurm where the cluster is a
research machine, Kubernetes where the same cluster also runs rollout engines,
environment fleets, and evaluation services, which RL makes likely.

The job specification below starts a 128-node pretraining job on Kubernetes. It
asks Kueue for admission through a queue, requires placement inside one network
block, and restarts every worker from the last checkpoint after a failure. The
container image is pinned by digest, which is part of the run identity.

```yaml
apiVersion: jobset.x-k8s.io/v1alpha2
kind: JobSet
metadata:
  name: pt-0042
  labels:
    kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: pretrain     # Kueue admits all workers or none
spec:
  failurePolicy:
    maxRestarts: 30                         # each restart resumes from the last checkpoint
  replicatedJobs:
  - name: workers
    template:
      spec:
        parallelism: 128                    # 128 nodes x 8 GPUs
        completions: 128
        backoffLimit: 0                     # one failed pod fails the Job; JobSet restarts all
        template:
          metadata:
            annotations:
              kueue.x-k8s.io/podset-required-topology: "cloud.provider.com/topology-block"
          spec:
            restartPolicy: Never
            containers:
            - name: trainer
              image: registry.example.com/train@sha256:4be1...   # pinned by digest
              command: ["bash", "-c"]
              args:
              - >-
                torchrun --nnodes=128 --nproc_per_node=8
                --node_rank=$JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX
                --master_addr=pt-0042-workers-0-0.pt-0042 --master_port=29500
                pretrain_gpt.py $MODEL_ARGS $PARALLEL_ARGS $DATA_ARGS $CKPT_ARGS
              resources:
                limits:
                  nvidia.com/gpu: 8
```

The topology level names a node label that the cluster administrator defines;
`cloud.provider.com/topology-block` is the placeholder Kueue's documentation
uses. The worker hostnames follow JobSet's pattern of JobSet name, replicated
Job name, Job index, and pod index, and `JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX` gives each pod its
node rank. On Slurm the same job is an `sbatch` script with the GPU request, a
warning signal before the time limit, and `--requeue`.

### The run identity

A number reported from a run is usable only if the run can be identified. The
run identity is the set of inputs that determine what the run computes: the code
commit and container digest, the data manifest digest, the model and optimizer
configuration, the parallel layout, the seeds, and the accelerator type. The
experiment tracker records it once, at launch, and every metric, checkpoint,
and evaluation carries the run identifier and the training step. A restart
after a failure is a new attempt of the same run, not a new run, provided that
it restores the same state; a change of layout on restart, which resharding
checkpoints permit, is recorded as a change to the identity because it can
change numerics. Two runs that differ in any field are different experiments,
however similar their names.

::: {.callout-note .dated}

## The checkpoint store

The third seam runs from the trainer to storage and back. A checkpoint holds the
complete state needed to continue: model weights, optimizer state, the
learning-rate schedule, random-number generator states, and the data loader's
position. Optimizer state dominates the size. With mixed-precision Adam, each
parameter carries a BF16 weight (2 bytes), an FP32 master copy (4 bytes), and
two FP32 moment estimates (8 bytes), so a full checkpoint holds about 14 bytes
per parameter, roughly 1 TB for a 70-billion-parameter model. The weights alone,
in BF16, are 140 GB.

Three techniques keep checkpointing cheap enough to do often. Each rank writes
only its own shard in parallel, as PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint and
Megatron's `torch_dist` format do, and the same formats can load the shards onto
a different parallel layout [@pytorch2026dcp; @nvidia2026megatronlm]; Orbax
fills the same role for JAX [@google2026orbax]. Saves are asynchronous: training
pauses only to copy the state from accelerator memory to host memory, and a
background process writes it out. Storage is tiered: frequent checkpoints go to
a fast local or scratch tier that keeps only the latest, and less frequent ones
go to a durable tier with a retention schedule. How often to save follows from
the checkpoint cost and the failure rate; @sec-machine-breaks derives the
interval that minimizes lost work, and @sec-orchestration-data-infra treats a
checkpoint as a distributed commit that is complete only when every shard and
the metadata are written.

In Megatron-LM, the whole policy is a set of flags on the trainer
[@nvidia2026megatronlm]:

```bash
CKPT_ARGS=(
  --save /lustre/ckpt/pt-0042            # durable tier
  --load /lustre/ckpt/pt-0042            # the same path: a restart resumes from the latest
  --ckpt-format torch_dist               # sharded; loads onto a different layout
  --async-save                           # training pauses only for the copy to host memory
  --use-persistent-ckpt-worker           # async saves of torch_dist run in this worker
  --save-interval 1000                   # durable checkpoint every 1,000 steps
  --save-retain-interval 10000           # keep every 10,000th; older ones are deleted
  --non-persistent-save-interval 100     # frequent checkpoint every 100 steps ...
  --non-persistent-ckpt-type global      # ... to a scratch directory that keeps the latest
  --non-persistent-global-ckpt-dir /scratch/ckpt/pt-0042
  --exit-signal-handler                  # on SIGTERM, save and exit cleanly
  --exit-on-missing-checkpoint           # a wrong --load path fails instead of starting over
)
```

The last flag closes a quiet failure: without it, a mistyped load path starts a
new run from random initialization under the old run's name.

### The failure budget

A long run needs a stated budget for time not spent training. The useful
fraction of wall-clock time, often called effective training time or
@gls-goodput, loses to four terms: pauses to save, work lost since the last
checkpoint when a failure strikes, time to detect the failure, and time to
restart and restore. @sec-machine-breaks models these terms; Meta reported more
than 90 percent effective training time for Llama 3 405B despite 419 unexpected
interruptions in 54 days [@grattafiori2024llama]. The budget becomes an
operating rule when each term has an owner and a measurement: a checkpoint
pause measured per save, a restore drill run before the long job starts and
after every change of layout or storage, a detection deadline for hangs as well
as crashes, and a per-week count of interruptions by cause. A run that falls
below its budget stops scaling up until the cause is known, because adding
nodes adds failures.

## The rollout fleet

The fourth seam exists only in RL. A policy generates trajectories, a reward
path scores them, the learner updates the weights, and the new weights must
reach the generators before the next round. The generators are rollout
engines: vLLM or SGLang replicas that batch many trajectories at once and
return, with each generated token, its token ID and log-probability, which the
learner needs to compute its update. @sec-training-agents separates the two
systems decisions this seam involves. Placement puts the learner and the rollout
engines on the same GPUs, **colocated**, or on separate pools,
**disaggregated**. Synchronization either waits for a whole batch of
trajectories before each update, **synchronous**, or lets generation continue
while the learner trains, **asynchronous**. This section covers the machinery
that implements those choices.

Weight synchronization is the mechanical core. When learner and engines share
GPUs, the engine releases its memory while the learner trains, the learner's
weights are resharded into the engine's layout, and the engine takes them over
CUDA inter-process communication (IPC) without a copy across the network. When
they are disaggregated, the learner broadcasts the weights to the engines over
NCCL or writes them to shared storage for the engines to load. vLLM exposes this
as a four-phase transfer API, initializing a transfer channel, starting an
update, transferring the weights in chunks over NCCL or CUDA IPC, and finishing
with post-processing such as quantization, together with a pause mode that
keeps in-flight requests while the weights change [@vllm2026rlapis]. SGLang
offers updates from disk, from tensors, or from a distributed group inside a
weight-update session, pauses generation by aborting, retracting, or holding
requests in place, and can report which weight version produced each token
[@sglang2026rl]. The transfer is not free: a 70-billion-parameter policy in
BF16 is 140 GB, and at 50 GB/s, one 400 Gb/s link, a full copy to one replica
takes about three seconds before any parallelism across links.

The per-token version attribution matters because asynchrony makes
**staleness** routine. A trajectory generated with weights $k$ versions older
than the learner's is off-policy by $k$ steps, and a long trajectory can span
several updates. The controls are practical ones. Every trajectory records the
policy version that produced each of its tokens, along with the engine's token
IDs and log-probabilities. The run sets a staleness bound and drops what exceeds
it. The loss corrects the remaining mismatch with a clipped or truncated
importance ratio between the learner's and the engine's probabilities
(@sec-training-agents). A mixture-of-experts policy also replays the engine's
expert routing in the learner, and the run logs the gap between the learner's
and the engine's log-probabilities for the same tokens, which stays nonzero even
in synchronous runs because the two use different kernels and precision
(@sec-training-to-reason).

The trade between the two synchronization modes is quantitative, and a small
simulation shows its shape. Rollout durations vary: a trajectory that ends in a
short answer takes a fraction of the time of one that runs to the length limit
or waits on a slow tool. The cell below draws each rollout's duration as a fixed
part $1-c$ plus an exponential tail of mean $c$, so the mean is always 1 and
$c$ is the coefficient of variation, the standard deviation over the mean. In
the synchronous mode, 64 slots each generate one trajectory, and the update
waits for the slowest. The idle share of slot time is then
$1 - 1/\mathbb{E}[\max]$, and for this distribution
$\mathbb{E}[\max] = (1-c) + c H_{64}$, where $H_{64} = \sum_{i=1}^{64} 1/i
\approx 4.74$ is the expected maximum of 64 unit exponentials. In the
asynchronous mode, each slot starts a new trajectory with the newest weights as
soon as its last one finishes, and every 64 finished trajectories make one
update. No slot waits, but a trajectory's lag, the number of updates between its
start and its use, is no longer zero. Each update advances the lag of the 63
trajectories still in flight, so the mean lag is exactly $(W-1)/B = 63/64$ for
$W = 64$ slots and a batch of $B = 64$, whatever the spread; only the tail of
the lag distribution grows with $c$. The cell asserts both closed forms against
the simulation and reports how many trajectories a bound of $K = 2$ versions
would drop.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import heapq
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

B = 64            # trajectories per policy update
W = 64            # rollout slots, each generating one trajectory at a time
K = 2             # staleness bound: drop trajectories more than K versions old
UPDATES = 400     # policy updates simulated for each spread value
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
H = np.sum(1 / np.arange(1, B + 1))           # harmonic number: E[max of B Exp(1)]

def durations(c, size):
    """Rollout time with mean 1: a fixed part 1 - c plus an exponential tail of mean c."""
    return (1 - c) + c * rng.exponential(1.0, size)

def synchronous(c):
    """Each update waits for the slowest of B rollouts; returns the idle share of slot time."""
    t = durations(c, (UPDATES, B))
    return 1 - t.sum() / (B * t.max(axis=1).sum())

def asynchronous(c):
    """Slots restart at once with the newest weights; every B finished rollouts make an update."""
    version, done, lags = 0, 0, []
    draws = iter(durations(c, W + (UPDATES + 20) * B))
    slots = [(next(draws), 0) for _ in range(W)]  # (finish time, version it started with)
    heapq.heapify(slots)
    while version < UPDATES + 20:
        now, v = heapq.heappop(slots)
        lags.append(version - v)                  # updates since this rollout started
        done += 1
        if done == B:
            version, done = version + 1, 0
        heapq.heappush(slots, (now + next(draws), version))
    return np.array(lags[20 * B:])                # drop the start-up transient

spread = np.linspace(0.05, 1.0, 12)
idle = np.array([synchronous(c) for c in spread])
idle_exact = 1 - 1 / ((1 - spread) + spread * H)
lags = [asynchronous(c) for c in spread]
mean_lag = np.array([l.mean() for l in lags])
p99_lag = np.array([np.percentile(l, 99) for l in lags])
dropped = np.array([(l > K).mean() for l in lags])

assert np.all(np.abs(idle - idle_exact) < 0.02)          # synchronous: the closed form holds
assert np.all(np.abs(mean_lag - (W - 1) / B) < 0.01)     # asynchronous: mean lag is (W-1)/B
assert dropped[0] == 0 and dropped[-1] > 0.05            # the tail, not the mean, grows

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(5.6, 5.6), sharex=True)
ax1.plot(spread, idle_exact, color="C0", label="synchronous, closed form")
ax1.plot(spread, idle, "o", color="C0", ms=4, label="synchronous, simulated")
ax1.plot(spread, 0 * spread, color="C1", label="asynchronous")
ax1.set(ylabel="idle share of rollout time", ylim=(-0.03, 1))
ax1.legend(fontsize=9, loc="upper left")
ax2.plot(spread, np.full_like(spread, (W - 1) / B), "--", color="C1", label="mean lag, closed form")
ax2.plot(spread, mean_lag, "o", color="C1", ms=4, label="mean lag, simulated")
ax2.plot(spread, p99_lag, "s-", color="C2", ms=4, label="99th percentile lag")
ax2.plot(spread, 0 * spread, color="C0", label="synchronous")
ax2.set(xlabel="rollout-time spread c (standard deviation / mean)",
        ylabel="policy versions behind", ylim=(-0.3, 6))
ax2.legend(fontsize=9, loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout()

for k in (0, 4, 8, 11):
    c, i, m, p, d = spread[k], idle[k], mean_lag[k], p99_lag[k], dropped[k]
    print(f"c = {c:.2f}: synchronous idle {i:4.0%}; asynchronous mean lag {m:.2f}, "
          f"99th percentile {p:.0f}, over K={K}: {d:4.1%}")
```
::::

The printed lines carry the argument. With a spread of only 5 percent, the
synchronous batch already leaves about 16 percent of slot time idle, because
the slowest of 64 draws sits well above the mean; with exponential durations,
$c = 1$, the idle share reaches $1 - 1/H_{64} \approx 79$ percent. The
asynchronous mode keeps every slot busy at a mean lag just under one version at
every spread, but its 99th-percentile lag climbs from 2 to 5 versions, and a
bound of two versions discards about 8 percent of trajectories at $c = 1$. Real
length distributions are often heavier-tailed than the exponential, and a cap on
generation length truncates them, so the measured spread of a workload, not a
default, should set both the synchronization mode and the bound. Partial
rollouts, which pause a long trajectory at the update and resume it with the new
weights, and over-sampling with early cutoff are further ways to cut the
synchronous tail at the cost of mixing versions inside one trajectory.

Placement adds its own arithmetic. Generating a token costs about $2N$ FLOPs for
a model of $N$ parameters, while training on it costs about $6N$ for the
forward and backward passes plus $2N$ to recompute the current policy's
log-probabilities, so the learner performs about four times the arithmetic of
the generators. Generation, however, runs far below peak, because decoding is
limited by memory bandwidth (@sec-serving-problem). At an assumed 40 percent
MFU for training and 5 percent for decoding, generation takes twice the GPU time
of training; at 10 percent, the two are equal. OpenRLHF's documentation puts
generation at 80 percent of RLHF training time [@openrlhf2026repo]. Either way,
the rollout pool usually needs at least as many GPUs as the learner, and in a
colocated layout the same GPUs alternate between the two roles.

### Frameworks

The open RL frameworks differ mainly in which training backend and rollout
engine they join, how they place them, and how far they go toward asynchrony.

| Framework | Training and rollout | Placement and synchronization | Built for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **verl** | FSDP, FSDP2, or Megatron learners; vLLM or SGLang rollouts [@verl2026repo] | Colocated hybrid engine by default; one-step-off and fully asynchronous trainers with a staleness threshold | Broad algorithm coverage from one node to hundreds of GPUs |
| **OpenRLHF** | DeepSpeed learners on Ray; vLLM rollouts [@openrlhf2026repo] | Shared or separate GPUs; asynchronous training by a flag | PPO-family and agent RL on a Ray cluster |
| **NeMo RL** | PyTorch DTensor or Megatron Core learners on Ray; vLLM or SGLang generation [@nemorl2026repo] | Colocated or separate; asynchronous GRPO | The NVIDIA stack and large mixture-of-experts models |
| **slime** | Megatron learners; SGLang rollouts behind a router [@slime2026repo] | Colocated or disaggregated; fully asynchronous rollout for long-tailed agent tasks | Large-scale RL with both engines' native arguments |
| **prime-rl** | FSDP2 learners; vLLM rollouts [@primerl2026repo] | Disaggregated and fully asynchronous, with a bound on off-policy steps | Agentic RL at scale with `verifiers` environments |
| **SkyRL** | FSDP or Megatron learners; vLLM, SGLang, or an OpenAI-compatible endpoint [@skyrl2026repo] | Synchronous, one-step-off, or fully asynchronous with in-flight weight updates | Long-horizon agents; SkyRL-Gym environments |
| **AReaL** | Separate training, inference, agent, and weight-update services [@areal2026repo; @fu2025areal] | Fully asynchronous with staleness-aware training | Agents that join online RL through a base URL |
| **TRL** | Transformers trainers; vLLM colocated or as a server [@hf2026trl; @hf2026trlvllm] | Synchronous, with an experimental asynchronous GRPO trainer that streams from a vLLM server | RL that fits one node or a few (@sec-training-practice) |

A framework is chosen by the engine pair the team already operates and by the
stage's shape. A Megatron shop training a large mixture-of-experts model reaches
for slime, NeMo RL, or verl's Megatron path; a team whose bottleneck is
environment latency on long agent tasks reaches for a fully asynchronous
design such as prime-rl, SkyRL, or AReaL; and a single node is served by TRL.
The framework's configuration is where the placement, synchronization, and
staleness decisions become reviewable. The run below, trimmed from prime-rl's
own software-engineering example, puts the learner and the rollout engines on
separate nodes, broadcasts weights over NCCL, bounds staleness, and caps the
number of episodes in flight, which is also the number of live sandboxes
[@primerl2026repo]:

```toml
max_steps = 1000
seq_len = 131072

[deployment]
type = "multi_node"
num_train_nodes = 4              # learner: FSDP2
num_infer_nodes = 1
num_infer_replicas = 4           # rollout engines: vLLM

[model]
name = "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-BF16"

[weight_broadcast]
type = "nccl"                    # learner to engines, once per update

[ckpt]
interval = 50

[trainer]
enable_router_replay = true      # replay the engine's expert routing in the learner

[orchestrator]
batch_size = 256                 # trajectories per update
group_size = 16                  # samples per task, for group-relative advantages
max_off_policy_steps = 32        # drop episodes more than 32 versions old

[orchestrator.concurrency]
max_inflight = 1536              # episodes in flight, and so live sandboxes

[[orchestrator.train.source]]
name = "scaleswe"
env.taskset.id = "scaleswe"      # tasks, environment image, and verifier
env.agent.harness.id = "rlm"

[orchestrator.eval]
interval = 20                    # held-out evaluation every 20 steps

[inference.vllm]
tensor_parallel_size = 8
enable_expert_parallel = true
enable_return_routed_experts = true   # the routing that router replay needs
```

::: {.callout-note .dated}

## Environments and verifiers

The fifth seam connects the rollouts to the world they act in. In RL with
verifiable rewards, the "environment" is a prompt and a checker, and both can
run inside the framework's own processes. In agentic RL, each trajectory needs
a live environment for as long as it runs: a repository with its test suite, a
tool server with its database, or a browser. The environment executes the
policy's actions, returns observations, and at the end hands its final state to
a verifier. @sec-training-agents covers where environments come from and why
they must be versioned like data; this section covers how they are served.

Environment servers present one of two interfaces. The first is a
Gymnasium-style pair of calls, `reset` and `step`, served over the network so
that environments run in their own containers: OpenEnv packages environments
this way [@openenv2026repo], the `verifiers` library defines environments,
their rubrics, and their datasets for prime-rl and for evaluation
[@verifiers2026repo], and SkyRL-Gym provides math, coding, search, and SQL
environments behind the Gymnasium API [@skyrl2026repo]. The second interface
inverts the call: an existing agent harness runs unchanged and reaches the
policy through an OpenAI-compatible base URL that the RL system serves, and the
system records the token IDs and log-probabilities behind each response. AReaL
uses this pattern to put agent applications into online RL [@areal2026repo],
and SkyRL accepts any OpenAI-compatible endpoint that supports weight sync as a
rollout engine [@skyrl2026repo]. The second interface is what makes the
training harness identical to the deployed one (@sec-the-harness), at the cost
of treating every harness release as a new environment revision.

The fleet behind either interface is sized by concurrency. Every trajectory in
flight holds one environment, so the in-flight cap in the RL configuration is
also the number of live sandboxes: 1,536 in the prime-rl example above. The
fleet runs on CPU nodes, often in a separate pool or a separate provider from
the GPUs, and its costs are start-up time, image pulls, and the long tail of
slow actions, which becomes the rollout tail the synchronous simulation
measured. DeepSeek's sandbox platform shows the scale this reaches: one
production unit of about 160 nodes serves about 3 million sandboxes a day, and
the platform keeps stateful rollout execution separate from preemptible GPU
training [@huang2026dsec].

Isolation is stricter than for a product sandbox, not looser. The code in these
environments is written by a policy that is being optimized to raise a score,
so an environment that exposes the answer, the test file, the network, or a
credential will be exploited, and the exploit becomes a learned behavior
(@gls-reward-hacking). Each environment gets its own filesystem, process
namespace, and network policy with default-deny egress; containers suffice for
trusted tasks, while code execution usually runs under gVisor or in microVMs
(@sec-agents-practice). The environment holds no credential that the task does
not require, and a tool that must reach an external system goes through a
brokered, scoped credential (@sec-security-authorization). The runtime-safety
controls of a deployed agent apply unchanged (@sec-runtime-safety).

The verifier runs outside the policy's writable boundary. Four kinds of scorer
are common: rule-based checkers, such as Math-Verify, which parses a
mathematical answer and compares it with the reference symbolically
[@mathverify2026repo]; test runs, which execute a hidden test suite in a fresh
copy of the final state rather than in the workspace the policy could edit;
reward models, served as a GPU service like any other model; and model judges,
served by the same kind of engine as the rollouts and budgeted like them. Each
scorer has a latency budget, because a slow verifier extends every trajectory,
and a determinism budget, because a flaky test is reward noise. Every
trajectory records the environment image, task, verifier, and judge revisions
that produced its reward, which is what lets a reward spike be traced to a
changed verifier rather than to a better policy.

::: {.callout-note .dated}

uses a BSD license [@openenv2026repo]. `verifiers` is at v0.3.1 under the MIT
license [@verifiers2026repo], and SkyRL-Gym ships inside the SkyRL repository

## The evaluation gate

The sixth seam decides which checkpoint leaves the run. Evaluation happens at
three cadences. During pretraining and mid-training, small suites and held-out
loss run on checkpoints every few thousand steps to catch a regression while it
is still cheap to roll back. At each stage boundary, a full suite decides whether
the stage's output becomes the next stage's input. Before release, the gate adds
safety evaluations and red teaming (@sec-safety-tuning), agent suites where the
model will act (@sec-evaluating-agents), and contamination checks against the
data manifest's decontamination registry (@sec-benchmarks).

A candidate is scored as it will be served. The checkpoint is converted to the
release format, loaded by the serving engine with the chat template and
generation defaults that will ship, and exposed behind an OpenAI-compatible
endpoint. The harness then talks to that endpoint rather than to the training
code: lm-evaluation-harness calls it through its `local-completions` and
`local-chat-completions` model types [@lmevalharness2026], and Inspect runs
agentic and safety evaluations against the same kind of endpoint
[@inspectai2026]. Scoring through the endpoint tests the conversion and the
serving configuration as well as the weights, which a score computed inside
the trainer cannot do.

```bash
# Serve the converted candidate as production will, then score it through the API.
vllm serve /release/pt-0042-step120000 --served-model-name candidate --port 8000 &
lm-eval run --model local-completions \
  --model_args model=candidate,base_url=http://localhost:8000/v1/completions,num_concurrent=32,tokenized_requests=False \
  --tasks gsm8k,ifeval --output_path results/candidate --log_samples
python gate.py results/baseline/results.json results/candidate/results.json
```

The gate itself is a few lines that compare the candidate's scores with fixed
floors and with the baseline's scores. The thresholds are written before the
run and live next to it, so no one can choose them after seeing the numbers.

```python
# gate.py: promote only if every gated metric holds its floor and none regresses
# beyond its tolerance plus two standard errors. The thresholds were fixed before the run.
import json
import sys

GATE = {  # task: (metric key in lm-eval results, floor, allowed drop against the baseline)
    "gsm8k": ("exact_match,strict-match", 0.80, 0.01),
    "ifeval": ("prompt_level_strict_acc,none", 0.75, 0.01),
}

def results(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        return json.load(f)["results"]

base, cand = results(sys.argv[1]), results(sys.argv[2])
failures = []
for task, (metric, floor, drop) in GATE.items():
    b, c = base[task][metric], cand[task][metric]
    se = cand[task].get(metric.replace(",", "_stderr,"))
    se = se if isinstance(se, float) else 0.0
    if c < floor:
        failures.append(f"{task}: {c:.3f} is below the floor {floor}")
    if c + 2 * se < b - drop:
        failures.append(f"{task}: {c:.3f} against the baseline {b:.3f}")
print("PROMOTE" if not failures else "REJECT\n" + "\n".join(failures))
sys.exit(1 if failures else 0)
```

The rule in the script is deliberately crude; @sec-statistical-reliability
explains how to size the suites and set a rule whose error rates are known.

### The promotion rule

The promotion rule is the contract of this seam. It names the suites, metrics,
floors, regression tolerances, and uncertainty treatment before the run starts
(@sec-operational-evaluation). It covers every class of behavior the release
could change: capability, instruction following, safety and refusal
calibration, and the no-change requirements that protect existing users. It is
applied to the candidate as served, never to a score logged by the trainer. Its
decision is recorded with the run identity, the candidate's digest, the suite
versions, and the name of the approver, and a candidate that fails is never
promoted by editing the rule. A rule that must change is changed for the next
run.

## The release artifact

The last seam turns a gated checkpoint into something others can run. A
training checkpoint is the wrong artifact to ship: it is sharded for a training
layout, holds FP32 master weights and optimizer state, and needs the training
code to load. The release is a conversion. It extracts the weights, writes them
in the serving precision as safetensors files, which hold raw tensors and a
header and cannot execute code on load [@safetensors2026format], and adds the
model configuration, the tokenizer files, the chat template, and the generation
defaults. TorchTitan can save in the Hugging Face layout directly
[@pytorch2026torchtitanrepo], and Megatron Bridge converts between Megatron and
Hugging Face checkpoints [@nvidia2026megatronlm]. Quantized builds and GGUF
files for local runtimes [@ggml2023gguf] are derived artifacts with their own
digests and their own parity checks (@sec-model-artifacts).

The conversion has one acceptance test: the converted artifact, loaded by the
serving engine, reproduces the evaluated behavior. Because the gate already
scored the converted artifact through the serving engine, the test reduces to
checking that the published files are byte-identical to the ones the gate saw.
The publisher then signs the release under the OpenSSF model signing
specification, which signs a manifest of every file's path and digest
[@openssf2025modelsigning], and pushes it to a model hub or an
OCI registry [@oci2025distribution]. The hand-off to serving is the start of
the application stack's lifecycle (@sec-serving-stack, @sec-deployment-lifecycle):
the release's digest becomes the identity that a serving system pins and that a
rollback restores.

## Three reference stacks

Most teams that train models fall into one of three archetypes by scale. The
rows are the layers of @fig-training-stack-arch; the entries are examples as of
September 2026 and starting points to adapt, not rankings.

| Layer | Post-training team on open weights (1 to 64 GPUs) | RL lab with an environment fleet (hundreds of GPUs) | Pretraining effort (thousands of GPUs) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Data** | Own demonstrations and preference pairs, public datasets, a manifest in the repository | Task sets with verifiers, environment images in a registry, synthetic data from a teacher model | DataTrove or NeMo Curator on a processing cluster; a corpus manifest; token shards on object storage or Lustre |
| **Compute and scheduling** | Rented nodes or a managed training API; Slurm or plain Kubernetes Jobs | Kubernetes with Kueue and JobSet, or Slurm; a separate CPU pool for environments | Reserved clusters with InfiniBand or RoCE; Slurm, or Kubernetes with Kueue's topology-aware scheduling |
| **Training runtime** | TRL, Axolotl, or Unsloth over FSDP2 or DeepSpeed (@sec-training-practice) | The RL framework's learner on FSDP2 or Megatron Core | Megatron Core, TorchTitan, or MaxText with a tuned parallel layout |
| **Post-training** | SFT and DPO; GRPO in TRL with colocated vLLM | verl, slime, prime-rl, SkyRL, or AReaL with vLLM or SGLang rollouts, asynchronous with a staleness bound | The RL lab's stack, run after mid-training |
| **Environments and rewards** | Rule checkers such as Math-Verify, in process | Sandboxes behind OpenEnv or `verifiers` interfaces; test runners and judge servers | As for the RL lab, at larger concurrency |
| **Checkpoints** | Full or adapter checkpoints on local disk, copied to object storage | Sharded asynchronous checkpoints of the learner, plus the data buffer's position | Asynchronous sharded checkpoints in fast and durable tiers, with restore drills |
| **Tracking and evaluation** | An experiment tracker; lm-evaluation-harness in CI | Per-step reward, length, and staleness statistics; held-out agent suites | Scheduled checkpoint evaluations; a written gate at every stage boundary |
| **Release** | Adapter or merged weights in safetensors, with a card | A post-trained model released through the pretraining effort's process, or its own | Converted, signed artifacts with model and system cards, a license, and staged access |

The columns share more than they differ. The same seams appear in all three,
and a team moving from the first column to the second mostly adds the rollout
fleet and the environment fleet; a team moving to the third mostly adds scale to
the data plane and to the failure budget. What changes most across the columns
is which seam fails first: data quality in the first, environment reliability
and staleness in the second, and hardware failure and checkpoint bandwidth in
the third.

## The arithmetic of a run

Four numbers size a run before any hardware is reserved: the compute, the
checkpoint footprint, the data footprint, and, for RL, the split between
generation and training.

**Compute.** A dense transformer with $N$ parameters trained on $D$ tokens
performs about $6ND$ floating-point operations: $2ND$ for the forward pass and
$4ND$ for the backward pass (@sec-scaling-laws). A 70-billion-parameter model on
15 trillion tokens needs

$$
6ND = 6 \times (7\times10^{10}) \times (1.5\times10^{13}) = 6.3\times10^{24}\ \text{FLOPs}.
$$

An H100 SXM delivers about 989 dense BF16 teraFLOPS at peak, half of the
datasheet's figure with sparsity [@nvidia2026h100]. At 40 percent MFU, each GPU
contributes $3.96\times10^{14}$ FLOPs per second, so the run needs
$1.59\times10^{10}$ GPU-seconds, or 4.4 million GPU-hours: 45 days on 4,096
GPUs before failures, and about 50 days at 90 percent effective training time.
The same formula checks against a published run: Llama 3 405B on 15.6 trillion
tokens gives $6ND = 3.79\times10^{25}$, which matches the reported
$3.8\times10^{25}$, and at the reported 400 teraFLOPs per GPU the run needs about
26 million GPU-hours, or 67 days on 16,384 GPUs of steady-state training
[@grattafiori2024llama].

**Checkpoints.** At 14 bytes per parameter, the 70-billion-parameter model's
full checkpoint is about 980 GB. Spread over 4,096 GPUs, each rank holds about
240 MB, so the copy to host memory that an asynchronous save waits for takes a
fraction of a second; the durable write then has until the next save to finish,
which at one save per hour is about 0.3 GB/s in aggregate. Retention decides
the storage: keeping every hourly checkpoint for 45 days would take about 1 PB,
while keeping the latest three full checkpoints and a 140 GB weights-only
snapshot every six hours for the evaluation history takes about 28 TB.

**Data.** Fifteen trillion tokens stored as 4-byte token IDs, needed once a
vocabulary exceeds 65,536 entries, occupy 60 TB of shards; 2-byte IDs would
halve that for a smaller vocabulary. The pool before filtering is an order of
magnitude larger: DataComp-LM's Common Crawl pool holds 240 trillion tokens
[@li2024dclm]. The read bandwidth is modest: 15 trillion tokens over 45 days is
3.9 million tokens per second, about 15 MB/s of token IDs for the whole cluster.
Storage for training is therefore sized by checkpoint bursts and retention far
more than by data reads, while storage for data processing is sized by the raw
pool.

**Rollouts against training.** For an RL run with the placement arithmetic of
the rollout fleet section, generation performs a quarter of the learner's
arithmetic but, at 5 percent decoding MFU against 40 percent for training, takes
twice its GPU time, and a synchronous batch with a wide length spread idles part
of that time as well. A first plan provisions the rollout pool at one to two
times the learner's GPUs and then measures, since the ratio moves with response
length, batch size, and the engine's utilization. The environment fleet is sized
separately, at one sandbox for each trajectory in flight.

## The model provider

A team that releases weights, or serves them to others, takes on obligations
that a team training for itself does not. They attach to the release and outlive
the run.

The first is a release gate beyond capability. A provider evaluates the
candidate for misuse and dangerous capabilities, red-teams it
(@sec-safety-tuning), and, if it has published a frontier safety framework,
applies that framework's thresholds before release (@sec-law-policy). Access can
be staged: weights for a smaller model, an API with monitoring for a larger one,
and trusted-access programs for capabilities that need them.

The second is documentation. A model card records intended uses, evaluation
conditions, and limitations [@mitchell2019modelcards], and a system card
describes the deployed system and its safeguards. Under the EU AI Act, a
provider of a general-purpose model has had to keep technical documentation,
inform downstream providers, adopt a copyright policy, and publish a summary of
training content since 2 August 2025, and training compute above $10^{25}$
FLOPs creates a rebuttable presumption of high-impact capability, which
classifies the model as posing systemic risk and adds further duties
[@euaiact2024; @eugpai2025]. The arithmetic above lands on both sides of that
line: the 70-billion-parameter example uses $6.3\times10^{24}$ FLOPs, while
Llama 3 405B used $3.8\times10^{25}$. The data manifest and the run identity are
what make the training-content summary and the documentation answerable.

The third is the license. A provider chooses between a standard permissive
license, such as Apache 2.0 or MIT, and a custom license with use restrictions
or thresholds, and the data's terms limit what it can grant; @sec-model-landscape
compares the licenses current releases use. The fourth is distribution: the
signed artifact of the previous section, published where users fetch models, or
served behind the provider's own API, which puts the whole application stack of
@sec-wiring-stack in front of the model. The fifth is deprecation. A provider
that serves a model publishes a notice period and what happens to requests after
retirement, which consumers must plan around (@sec-choosing-model), and decides
how long to keep the retired weights.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

Anthropic has committed to preserving the weights of every publicly released
model, and of models deployed for significant internal use, for at least the
lifetime of the company, and to producing a post-deployment report when a model
is deprecated [@anthropic2025preservation].
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow
The serving engine reaches back into training twice. In RL, the rollout engine
is a serving engine, so its kernels, precision, and expert routing define the
behavior policy that the learner must correct for. At release, the serving
engine is the loader the artifact must satisfy, so the tokenizer, chat template,
and precision chosen in training become an interface every downstream consumer
depends on. A training stack that treats serving as someone else's problem
learns about both constraints late: once as an unexplained gap between the
learner's and the engine's probabilities, and once as a release that scores
differently from its checkpoint.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
Three choices are unsettled. Synchronous RL keeps every sample on-policy and
wastes GPU time on the length tail; asynchronous RL recovers the time and pays
in staleness and correction terms, and published comparisons cover a few
workloads each (@sec-training-agents). Integrated frameworks join a learner and
a rollout engine and move quickly with them; composing engines through their
native weight-update APIs keeps each engine current but moves the integration
work to the team. And the line between building and renting moves with each
managed service: a training API such as Tinker runs the loop's arithmetic on the
provider's accelerators while the team writes the loop
[@thinkingmachines2025tinker], which leaves data, environments, and gates with
the team. The seams in this chapter are the part expected to outlast any of
these answers.
:::
